title: What If Money Weighed Four Tons? On One Island It Does

scenes.text: What if your money weighed four tons? On the island of Yap, some of it does.
Yap's rai are limestone discs with a hole in the middle, up to twelve feet across.
The stone was quarried on Palau and brought 400 kilometers across open ocean by canoe and bamboo raft.
Nobody moves a big one to pay with it. The island simply remembers who owns it now.
One stone sank on the way home. Everyone agreed it was still down there, so it kept being spent.
About 6,000 remain. Money on the seabed sounds absurd, until you remember your bank balance is also just something everyone agrees on.

description:
What if your money weighed four tons? On Yap, in Micronesia, the traditional money is rai: discs of limestone with a hole in the centre, the largest 3.6 meters across and about 4,000 kilograms.
The stone was quarried on Palau, some 400 km away, and carried home by canoe and bamboo raft. A big rai is rarely moved; it changes hands when the island's oral history records a new owner, for things like marriages, inheritance and political deals. One stone that sank at sea went on being traded because everyone agreed it still existed. About 6,000 remain on the island, alongside modern currency for everyday use.
What should we run through next?
first_comment: A stone's value came partly from its story: how hard the voyage was, and who had owned it. What should money be made of? Drop your own what-if below.
